front: State **Newton’s first law**.
back: An object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it.

front: State **Newton’s second law** in two forms.
back: $F = ma$ for constant mass; more generally, resultant force = rate of change of momentum, $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$.

front: Three properties of a Newton’s **third-law** force pair?
back: Equal in size, opposite in direction, act on **different** objects — and they are the same type of force.

front: Are weight and the normal force on a resting book a third-law pair?
back: No. Both act on the book, and they are different types of force. They balance because the book is in equilibrium.

front: Static vs dynamic friction?
back: Static friction matches the applied force up to a maximum $\mu_s F_N$. Once sliding, dynamic friction is $\mu_d F_N$, usually smaller.

front: Define **linear momentum**. Unit?
back: $p = mv$, a vector. Unit kg m s⁻¹ (equivalent to N s).

front: What is **impulse**, and how do you find it from a graph?
back: Impulse $= F\Delta t = \Delta p$. It is the **area under a force–time graph**.

front: When is momentum conserved?
back: When no external resultant force acts on the system (an isolated system).

front: What makes a collision **elastic**?
back: Total kinetic energy is conserved. (Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system.)

front: Centripetal acceleration: size and direction?
back: $a = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2 r$, towards the centre of the circle.

front: What is a **centripetal force**?
back: The resultant force towards the centre needed for circular motion, $F = mv^2/r$ — supplied by a real force (tension, friction, gravity…), not an extra one.

front: Link angular velocity ω to period and speed.
back: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f$, and $v = \omega r$.

front: Mass vs weight?
back: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and resistance to acceleration — a scalar, the same everywhere. Weight $W = mg$ (N) is the gravitational force on it — a vector that depends on $g$.

front: What is **translational equilibrium**?
back: The resultant force on the object is zero, so it is at rest or moves at constant velocity.

front: Which force goes into $F = ma$?
back: The **resultant** (net) force — the vector sum of all forces on the object, not any single force.

front: What belongs on a free-body diagram?
back: Only forces acting **on** the chosen object, each drawn from the object as a labelled arrow. Never both forces of a third-law pair (they act on different objects).

front: Which way does friction act?
back: Parallel to the surfaces, opposing the **relative** motion (or the tendency to move) between them. It can point forwards — e.g. on a driven wheel or a walking foot.

front: Friction equations and what $\mu$ depends on?
back: Static: $F_f \le \mu_s F_N$. Sliding: $F_f = \mu_d F_N$. $\mu$ depends on the two surfaces; it has no unit and (in this model) is independent of contact area.

front: Normal force on a person of mass $m$ in a lift accelerating upwards at $a$?
back: $F_N - mg = ma \Rightarrow F_N = m(g + a)$ — the scale reads more than $mg$. Accelerating down: $F_N = m(g - a)$.

front: A ball hits a wall at $u$ and rebounds at $v$. Size of the change in momentum?
back: $m(v + u)$, not $m(v - u)$ — momentum is a vector and its direction reverses.

front: Kinetic energy in terms of momentum?
back: $E_k = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$. For equal momentum, the lighter object has more kinetic energy.

front: How do airbags and crumple zones reduce injury?
back: They increase the collision time $\Delta t$ for the same $\Delta p$, so the average force $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$ is smaller.

front: Elastic vs inelastic vs perfectly inelastic collision?
back: Elastic: $E_k$ conserved. Inelastic: some $E_k$ transferred to other forms. Perfectly inelastic: the objects stick together (maximum $E_k$ lost). Momentum is conserved in all three (isolated system).

front: Two objects at rest are pushed apart by an explosion. What happens to momentum and kinetic energy?
back: Total momentum stays zero: the parts move off with equal and opposite momenta ($m_1v_1 = m_2v_2$). Kinetic energy increases, coming from chemical or elastic energy.

front: Why is an object in uniform circular motion accelerating?
back: Its speed is constant but its **direction** changes continuously, so its velocity changes. The acceleration points to the centre.

front: A ball on a string is released mid-swing. Which way does it go, and why?
back: Along the **tangent** at that point — no force now acts horizontally, so it continues in a straight line. There is no outward “centrifugal force”.

front: Mass on a string in a vertical circle: tension at the top and bottom?
back: Top: $T + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Bottom: $T - mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The string stays taut at the top only if $v \ge \sqrt{gr}$.

front: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road?
back: Static friction between the tyres and the road, so $\mu_s mg \ge \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ sets the maximum safe speed $v = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$.

front: Unit of angular velocity ω, and a common error?
back: rad s⁻¹. Using degrees, or revolutions per minute, in $v = \omega r$ or $a = \omega^2 r$ gives wrong answers — convert first.
